newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch aim for draft EU treaty by May.
newsitem.headline: Dutch aim for draft EU treaty by May.

text.p: The Netherlands said on Tuesday that it hoped to have prepared a full draft European Union treaty by May, paving the way for agreement at a mid-June EU summit in Amsterdam.

"The (EU) presidency has to decide whether to come forward with a full (draft) text. No firm decisions have been taken but, in terms of timing, that will be in April or May," Dutch deputy foreign minister Michiel Patijn told reporters after chairing his first informal session of the treaty negotiating group.

The Dutch, who currently hold the EU presidency, are keen to complete key reforms of the 15-member bloc's institutions for inclusion in a new treaty in June, although privately they fear that agreement could be delayed by British elections due by May.
Several EU members believe they could make more progress on Europe with a new British government if, as widely expected, the ruling Conservatives lose the election.

The current British government is opposed to many proposals supported by other EU countries within the inter-governmental conference (IGC) negotiations, the forum charged with reforming key EU bodies ahead of a planned expansion into eastern Europe.
"We have organised our work very thoroughly. We will work on the basis of the Irish (interim) paper, which has already agreed three-quarters of the (draft treaty) text," Patijn said.
Ireland was EU president for the second half of 1996.

"At some stage we have to go through all the Irish text proposals, accept or amend them, fill in the blank spaces and then present the whole as a basis for the final stage of the negotiations," Patijn said.
He said he hoped there would be some stimulus to this at a special meeting of EU foreign ministers in Rome on March 25.
Patijn said the key to the IGC talks was reform of EU institutions so they could cope better with more members.
EU states are divided over the size, structure and role of the executive European Commission and many want to change the voting procedures in the Council of Ministers.
Patijn said that, while he was more optimistic on some points, these issues remain divisive and politically sensitive.

The IGC negotiating group will meet twice a month for full two-day sessions, Patijn said, with the clear aim of preparing the ground for a June treaty and not disrupting the bloc's tight timetable for Economic and Monetary Union and formal enlargement talks with potential new members.
However, Luxembourg, which takes over the EU presidency in July, has already set aside two dates for crisis summits should the Dutch fail to broker an Amsterdam Treaty in June.
